title: Math for ML: vectors, matrices, gradients, numerics
summary: The linear algebra, calculus and numerics an AI engineer actually uses: similarity search, shapes and einsum, least squares, SVD/low-rank (LoRA intuition), gradients you can check, gradient descent, and float formats (fp16/bf16/int8). Intuition from 3Blue1Brown, rigour from single MIT 18.06SC sessions, and build-it practice from rohitg00 Phase 01. Needs NumPy basics; can run alongside M04. Full 18.06SC, MML book, 18.S096 and Boyd are the optional Deep track.

units.title: Vectors, dot product, similarity

You can compute L1/L2 norms, distances and cosine similarity in NumPy without library helpers.
You can explain why unit-normalised embeddings make dot product, cosine and L2 rankings agree.

practice.title: Similarity search from scratch
practice.brief: In NumPy (no np.linalg.norm, no sklearn in the implementation) write l1, l2, cosine and top_k(query, matrix, k). Build bag-of-words vectors for 1,000 sentences and search them. Verify against sklearn.metrics.pairwise.cosine_similarity, then normalise every row and show L2 ranking == cosine ranking. Reference build: rohitg00 Phase 01 lessons 01 and 14.
practice.done_when: Your functions match sklearn to 1e-9 on 100 random pairs, and a printed check shows identical top-10 lists for L2 and cosine on unit-normalised vectors.
practice.autograder: pytest: assert np.allclose(cosine(a,b), sklearn cosine_similarity) for 100 random pairs

quiz.prompt: Cosine similarity of a and 2a is:
quiz.explain: Cosine ignores length; a and 2a point the same way, so the angle is 0 and cos 0 = 1.

quiz.prompt: For unit vectors a and b, ‖a−b‖² equals:
quiz.explain: ‖a−b‖² = ‖a‖² + ‖b‖² − 2a·b = 2 − 2a·b, so smaller distance ⇔ larger dot product.

quiz.prompt: The dot product of two orthogonal vectors is:
quiz.explain: Perpendicular vectors have zero projection on each other.

quiz.prompt: When would you use Mahalanobis distance instead of Euclidean distance?
options: When features have different scales and are correlated with each other
When you need a faster computation than L2
When features are all binary (0 or 1)
When you are comparing strings instead of vectors
quiz.explain: Mahalanobis distance accounts for the covariance structure of the data, decorrelating and normalizing features before computing L2 distance. It correctly handles features at different scales and with correlations, whereas Euclidean distance treats all dimensions equally. (Adapted from rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch Phase 01 lesson 14-norms-and-distances quiz.json, MIT licence.)

quiz.prompt: Why do most vector databases normalise embeddings and then use dot product instead of cosine?
rubric: States that for unit vectors dot product equals cosine similarity
Mentions dot product is cheaper (no per-query norm division) and supported by fast inner-product indexes
Notes normalisation happens once at index time
Optional: notes ranking by L2 is then equivalent too

quiz.prompt: A 5×3 matrix has rank at most:
quiz.explain: Rank ≤ min(rows, cols).

quiz.prompt: Least squares finds the vector in col(X) closest to y, i.e. it:
quiz.explain: The residual y − Xŵ is orthogonal to the column space.

quiz.prompt: Duplicated features make XᵀX:
quiz.explain: Linearly dependent columns drop the rank, so XᵀX has no inverse.

quiz.prompt: A matrix has condition number kappa = 10^8. You are using float64 (~15 digits of precision). How many digits of the solution can you trust?
options: Zero digits — the solution is meaningless
quiz.explain: You lose approximately log10(kappa) digits of precision. With kappa = 10^8, you lose about 8 digits from float64's ~15 digits, leaving about 7 trustworthy digits. If kappa approaches 10^16, the solution becomes meaningless in float64. (Adapted from rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch Phase 01 lesson 17-linear-systems quiz.json, MIT licence.)

quiz.prompt: For Av = λv, v is:
options: A direction only scaled by A
quiz.explain: Eigenvectors keep their direction; λ is the scale factor.

quiz.prompt: PCA's first component is the direction of:
quiz.explain: PCA orders directions by explained variance (largest singular value first).

quiz.prompt: A rank-8 update to a 4096×4096 matrix as B(4096×8)·A(8×4096) has how many parameters?
Why does sklearn implement PCA using SVD instead of eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix?
options: SVD produces different results that are more accurate for ML
SVD is easier to parallelize on GPUs
SVD works directly on the data matrix without forming the covariance matrix, avoiding squaring the condition number and improving numerical stability
SVD does not require centering the data
quiz.explain: Forming A^T*A squares the singular values (and condition number). If A has singular values [1000, 0.001], A^T*A has eigenvalues [10^6, 10^-6] -- 6 digits of precision lost. SVD avoids this by working directly on A. (Adapted from rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch Phase 01 lesson 11-singular-value-decomposition quiz.json, MIT licence.)

quiz.prompt: Explain what truncated SVD throws away, and why that is often acceptable.

Gives an ML example (compression, denoising, LoRA, embeddings)

practice.brief: Write numerical_derivative(f, x, h) using central differences. Compare with your hand-derived derivatives of x³, sin(x²), log(1+eˣ) and sigmoid. Plot |error| vs h from 1e-1 to 1e-12 on log–log axes.

quiz.prompt: d/dx of sigmoid σ(x) is:
quiz.explain: Differentiate 1/(1+e⁻ˣ) and rewrite in terms of σ.

quiz.prompt: If y = f(g(x)), dy/dx =
quiz.explain: Chain rule: outer derivative evaluated at the inner function, times inner derivative.

quiz.prompt: Central-difference error scales as:
quiz.explain: First-order terms cancel symmetrically; forward differences are O(h).

quiz.prompt: What is the numerical (central difference) approximation for f'(x)?
quiz.explain: The central difference (f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / (2h) is more accurate than the forward difference because it averages the slope on both sides of x, canceling out the leading error term. quiz.prompt: Why does the finite-difference estimate get worse when h becomes extremely small?

Round-off error grows like ε/h
Contrasts with truncation error that shrinks with h
Names a sensible h range (≈1e-5 to 1e-7 in float64)

quiz.prompt: Why does PyTorch use reverse-mode autodiff (backpropagation) instead of forward-mode?
options: Forward mode cannot handle non-linear functions
Reverse mode computes all gradients in one backward pass, while forward mode needs one pass per input variable -- neural networks have millions of inputs but one loss output
Reverse mode is more numerically accurate
quiz.explain: Neural networks have millions of weight inputs but produce a single scalar loss. Reverse mode needs one backward pass total. Forward mode would need one pass per weight -- millions of passes -- making it impractical. (Adapted from rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch Phase 01 lesson 05-chain-rule-and-autodiff quiz.json, MIT licence.)

quiz.prompt: Stable softmax subtracts:
quiz.explain: Makes the largest exponent exp(0)=1 so nothing overflows; probabilities are unchanged.

quiz.prompt: bf16 vs fp16: bf16 has
quiz.explain: bf16 keeps fp32's 8-bit exponent with a 7-bit mantissa; fp16 has 5 exponent bits and 10 mantissa bits.
0.1 and 0.2 are not exactly representable in binary.

quiz.prompt: In the stable softmax implementation, why do you subtract max(logits) before exponentiating?
options: It normalizes the logits to have zero mean
It converts logits from float16 to float32
It makes the output probabilities more uniform
It prevents exp() from overflowing by ensuring the largest exponent is 0
quiz.explain: After subtracting max(logits), the largest value is 0 and exp(0) = 1, which cannot overflow. All other values are negative, so their exponentials are less than 1. The probabilities are mathematically identical to the naive version. (Adapted from rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch Phase 01 lesson 13-numerical-stability quiz.json, MIT licence.)

Speed: decoding is memory-bandwidth bound so fewer bytes → faster
Cost: quantization error can reduce quality; needs evaluation

Run it on one public dataset and write a one-page README with plots (loss curves, LR sweep, one SVD/PCA figure). Pass: ≥ 7/10 with no 0s.
